To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a linear model using the body mass index as the only independent variable is the most convenient and best model for the prediction of material equivalent chest wall parameters, that the average chest wall parameters are sufficient to describe the chest wall at 59.5 keV and 185.8 keV, but are not sufficient at 17 kev, and that, in the future, the use of germanium detectors for lung monitoring should be restricted to 59.5–185.7 kev.

the average male worker chest wall thickness was 27 mm, the average fat fraction was 25%, and the material equivalent chest thickness can be estimated to an accuracy of 3.5 mm using the linear function: PMECWT = 0.45 BMI − 2.4.

the average male chest wall thickness in the French nuclear industry is 27 ± 5 mm and that a linear function of BMI provides a good approximation of the material equivalent thickness at 59.5 keV and 185.77 keV.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the chest wall thickness is an important factor to consider in lung monitoring, but that it is not necessary to use the equivalent material chest wall thickness, and the average chest wall can be used instead.

for lung monitoring with germanium detectors, the average chest wall can be used instead of material equivalent chest wall, and the average chest wall is well predicted by a linear function of body mass index.

for the purpose of in vivo lung monitoring, it is sufficient to use the average chest wall and fat thickness for all three energies, with an accuracy of ±3 mm and ±5%, respectively, for the 59.5 keV and 185.6 keV energies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the average chest wall can be used to predict PMECW thickness and X5050 at 185.7 and 59.5 keV, but not at 17 ke V.
the average chest wall is the most suitable parameter to predict the material equivalent chest walls at 59.5 or 185.7keV.
a simple linear function of the subject’s body mass index provides a good estimate of the chest wall thickness for lung monitoring with germanium detectors.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a simple linear model can be used for the calculation of the material equivalent thickness of the chest wall, and that the average chest wall is an adequate substitute for the equivalent thickness of the wall at 59.5 keV and above.
the use of a single average value of the material equivalent thickness for the whole population is not appropriate for the calculation of the effective dose.

the chest wall thickness can be predicted with a reasonable degree of accuracy using anthropometric measurements and that the fat fraction can be ignored when the chest wall thickness is calculated using an equivalent material at energies above 59.5 keV.
